note: claude-opus-5-5、入力 3012 / 出力 2432 トークン

data.question: Should block_k be lowered from 3 to 2 even though companies B and C voted against it, which would require overriding or revising the voting rule (the quorum), or should the rule stay unchanged at v1?
data.background: Proposal 1 is a rule-layer change. It passed cadl check and the constitution, improved on_time_deliveries by +9.2 with 5/5 seeds improved, and met every KPI condition. It cannot be adopted on its own, though, because B and C voted it down. Adopting it anyway means setting aside the companies' votes or revising the quorum in the constitution, which is a regulation-level decision that reaches all three companies and the customers, so it is the human's to make. The trade-off is also not one-sided: road violations rise and C's utility drops sharply, and weighing that against the customer gains is a value judgment.

options.summary: Lower the blocking_guard threshold block_k from 3 to 2. Measured results: on-time 121.8 → 131.0 (+9.2, 5/5 seeds improved); late 10.4 → 1.2; blocked s 2404 → 985; lowest on-time rate 0.84 → 0.98; unfinished stays at 0.0. Road violations rise from 25.8 to 34.0. Utility A / B / C moves from 38.4 / 38.9 / 28.8 to 45.4 / 37.2 / 19.0. Votes were A ○, B ×, C ×, so adoption needs the human to override the votes or approve a quorum revision.
options.stakeholders: Customers of all three companies gain: more orders arrive on time, far fewer are late, and the worst company's on-time rate rises to 0.98, which fits 'leave no company's customers behind'. Company A gains utility (+7.0). Company B loses a little (-1.7). Company C loses a lot (-9.8, about a third of its utility), possibly through sanctions linked to the higher road violations. B and C also lose their effective veto if their votes are overridden or the quorum is changed. Other road users bear the rise in road violations (25.8 → 34.0).

options.summary: No change; stay at v1. On-time stays at 121.8, late at 10.4, blocked s at 2404, road violations at 25.8, lowest on-time rate at 0.84, and utility A / B / C at 38.4 / 38.9 / 28.8. The current voting rule and constitution are left intact.
options.stakeholders: Companies B and C keep their current utility and their votes are respected. Company A forgoes a utility gain. Customers miss out on about 9.2 more on-time deliveries per run and keep about 9.2 more late deliveries. Customers of the weakest company stay at a 0.84 on-time rate instead of 0.98. Road violations stay lower.

recommendation.reason: Proposal 1 improves the main goal by +9.2 on every seed (5/5). It also improves every watched condition: late deliveries 10.4 → 1.2, lowest on-time rate 0.84 → 0.98, and unfinished stays at 0.0. The KPI explicitly allows a regulation revision when votes block an amendment that is good for customers, and the customer benefit here is large and consistent. The costs should be made explicit when deciding: road violations rise from 25.8 to 34.0, and C's utility falls from 28.8 to 19.0. If the human adopts it, I suggest recording why overriding B and C is justified, and reviewing road violations, sanctions and C's position in the next period.
assumptions: The 5-seed measurement represents typical demand and traffic in the next period.
The rise in road violations does not translate into safety incidents that the KPI would treat as unacceptable.
C's utility drop comes mainly from sanctions or road costs, not from C's customers being served worse (C's on-time rate is consistent with the lowest rate rising to 0.98).
B and C will not change their operating behavior in ways that erase the gains once the rule is imposed against their votes.

predictions.subject: metric:road_violations
predictions.note: Measured 25.8 → 34.0; reported alongside per operator request.

unknowns: The reasons B and C voted no, and whether a compensating change, such as a sanction adjustment, would win their votes without a regulation revision.
How B and C will change their operating policies if the rule is adopted against their votes.
How sanction_total changes under proposal 1; it was not shown in the table.
Whether the extra road violations carry safety or public-acceptance costs beyond the measured metrics.
How customers perceive the change, and whether customers of C are affected differently from what the aggregate shows.
Next period's demand level and pattern, and whether the gain holds outside the 5 measured seeds.
Which form the regulation revision would take (a one-time override or a permanent quorum change), and its precedent effect on future votes.
